fact_text: As a US citizen relocating from Seattle to Quito, you remain subject to US federal income tax on your worldwide income and must continue filing a US return (Form 1040) each year while living in Ecuador.
evidence_quote: You are subject to tax on worldwide income from all sources and must report all taxable income and pay taxes according to the Internal Revenue Code.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Many movers assume leaving the US ends US tax filing; US citizens are taxed on worldwide income regardless of country of residence.

fact_text: US tax benefits for Americans abroad (the foreign earned income exclusion and the foreign tax credit) are only available if you actually file a US tax return; they are not automatic.
evidence_quote: Many Americans living abroad qualify for special tax benefits, such as the foreign earned income exclusion and foreign tax credit, but they can only get them by filing a U.S. return.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The FEIE/FTC do not apply automatically; failing to file forfeits them even if you would otherwise owe no US tax.

fact_text: Once your tax home is in Ecuador you may qualify to exclude your foreign earned income from US tax using the foreign earned income exclusion (claimed on Form 2555), subject to inflation-adjusted annual limits.
evidence_quote: you may qualify to exclude your foreign earnings from income up to an amount that is adjusted annually for inflation

fact_text: To qualify for the foreign earned income exclusion via the physical presence test, you must be physically present in a foreign country (e.g. Ecuador) for at least 330 full days during a 12-month period.
evidence_quote: You meet the physical presence test if you are physically present in a foreign country or countries 330 full days during any period of 12 consecutive months including some part of the year at issue.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The 330-day count is strict; days over international waters during the Seattle->Quito move do not count toward the total.

fact_text: If the total value of your foreign (e.g. Ecuadorian) financial accounts exceeds USD 10,000 at any point in the calendar year, you must file an FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) reporting those accounts.
evidence_quote: A United States person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file an FBAR if the aggregate value of the foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The FBAR obligation is triggered by an aggregate $10,000 threshold and applies even to accounts that generate no income.

fact_text: The FBAR is filed electronically through the BSA E-Filing System and is due by April 15, the same as your federal return.
evidence_quote: Taxpayers should file a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) electronically by April 15 using the BSA e-filing system.

fact_text: Washington State currently has no individual income tax, so leaving Seattle triggers no Washington State income-tax exit filing for your relocation to Quito.
evidence_quote: Washington does not currently have an individual income tax.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Movers from income-tax states often expect a state exit/part-year return; Washington has no individual income tax so there is no state filing obligation on departure. Note a new 9.9% tax on AGI over $1 million takes effect Jan 1, 2028.

fact_text: There is no US-Ecuador Social Security totalization agreement: Ecuador does not appear on SSA's list of countries with which the US has a totalization agreement, so both the US and Ecuador may levy social-security contributions on the same work without coordination.
evidence_quote: they eliminate dual Social Security taxation, the situation that occurs when a worker from one country works in another country and is required to pay Social Security taxes to both countries on the same earnings

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Ecuador is absent from SSA's published list of totalization-agreement countries (Italy through Romania); with no agreement, the anti-double-taxation protection described by SSA does not apply to the US->Ecuador corridor and dual social-contribution liability is possible.

fact_text: You must keep your US Social Security number (SSN) active for tax filing: every person who files a US tax return needs an SSN or ITIN, and this requirement continues while you live in Ecuador.
evidence_quote: Each taxpayer who files, or is claimed as a dependent on, a U.S. tax return will need a social security number (SSN) or individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN).

fact_text: Living in Ecuador on the regular due date, you get an automatic 2-month extension to file your US return (to June 15 on a calendar year) without requesting it, though interest still accrues on unpaid tax from the regular April due date.
evidence_quote: you are allowed an automatic 2-month extension to file your return without requesting an extension

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The automatic 2-month extension only extends the filing date, not payment; interest still runs on tax unpaid after the regular April due date.
